items.title: Who rules Iran
items.sum: Iran is an Islamic republic in which an unelected Supreme Leader has the final say over the armed forces, the courts and state media. An elected president and parliament run the government within limits set by clerical councils. Since March 2026 the Supreme Leader has been Mojtaba Khamenei.
items.detail:
Supreme Leader: The top post, held for life. Ali Khamenei held it from June 1989 until he was killed on 28 February 2026; on 8–9 March 2026 the Assembly of Experts named his son Mojtaba Khamenei. The leader commands the armed forces and appoints the heads of the judiciary, the military and state broadcasting, and half of the Guardian Council.

Clerical councils: The Assembly of Experts, 88 clerics elected for eight years and chaired by Mohammad-Ali Movahedi Kermani, chooses the leader and can in theory remove him. The Guardian Council, six clerics named by the leader and six jurists approved by parliament and led by Ahmad Jannati, vets every candidate for elected office and can veto laws. The Expediency Council, chaired by Sadegh Amoli Larijani, settles disputes between parliament and the Guardian Council and advises the leader.

Elected bodies: The president is elected for four years and runs the government and the economy. Masoud Pezeshkian has held the post since July 2024, after Ebrahim Raisi died in a helicopter crash in May 2024; Abbas Araghchi is foreign minister. The 290-seat parliament (Majlis) is led by speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf.

Judiciary: The head of the judiciary is appointed by the leader. Gholam-Hossein Mohseni-Ejei has held the post since July 2021.

Security council: The Supreme National Security Council, chaired by the president, sets defence, security and nuclear policy, subject to the leader's approval. Its secretary Ali Larijani was killed on 17 March 2026 and was replaced by Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr; on 9 August 2026 Mohsen Rezaei, a former commander of the Revolutionary Guards, took over.

Armed forces: Iran has two militaries: the regular army (Artesh), commanded by Amir Hatami since June 2025, and the Revolutionary Guards (IRGC), commanded by Ahmad Vahidi since 1 March 2026. The General Staff above both has been led by Ali Abdollahi since 10 August 2026. The Basij militia, part of the IRGC, has been led by Hossein Taeb since August 2026.

items.title: The 1953 coup and the 1979 revolution
items.sum: In 1953 a coup backed by the US and Britain toppled Prime Minister Mohammad Mosaddegh and strengthened the Shah. In 1979 a mass revolution ended the monarchy and Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini founded the Islamic Republic. Months later students seized the US embassy and held 52 Americans for 444 days.
items.detail:
1953: Mosaddegh nationalised the British-run oil industry in 1951. On 19 August 1953 he was overthrown in a coup organised by the CIA and Britain's MI6 with royalist officers, and Mohammad Reza Shah ruled with growing power. The CIA acknowledged its role in documents released in 2013.

The Shah: He pushed rapid modernisation and land reform from 1963 and ruled through the SAVAK secret police. Khomeini, a senior cleric who led opposition to him, was exiled in 1964.

Revolution: Protests and strikes grew through 1978. The Shah left Iran on 16 January 1979, Khomeini returned from exile on 1 February, and the monarchy fell on 11 February. After a referendum, the Islamic Republic was declared on 1 April 1979. A constitution approved in December 1979 placed a senior cleric, the Supreme Leader, above elected officials, under Khomeini's doctrine of guardianship of the jurist (velayat-e faqih).

Hostage crisis: On 4 November 1979 students loyal to Khomeini stormed the US embassy in Tehran and took its staff hostage. 52 Americans were held for 444 days. A US rescue mission failed in April 1980, and the US cut diplomatic relations, which have never been restored. The hostages were freed on 20 January 1981 under the Algiers Accords.

Consolidation: In the early 1980s the new rulers pushed out or crushed rival groups, from liberals to leftists and the MEK. Khomeini died on 3 June 1989, and the Assembly of Experts chose Ali Khamenei to succeed him.

items.title: The Iran–Iraq war
items.sum: Iraq under Saddam Hussein invaded Iran in September 1980. The war lasted almost eight years, killed hundreds of thousands and ended without a winner, and it still shapes how Iran's leaders think about defence.
items.detail:
The invasion: Iraq invaded on 22 September 1980, hoping to seize the oil province of Khuzestan while Iran was weakened by the revolution. Iran halted the advance, retook Khorramshahr in May 1982 and then carried the war into Iraq.

The long war: The fighting settled into trench warfare. Iran sent waves of young volunteers, many from the Basij, against Iraqi lines. Iraq used chemical weapons against Iranian troops and, at Halabja in March 1988, against Iraqi Kurds. Both sides fired missiles at each other's cities and attacked oil tankers in the Gulf.

The US: In the tanker war the US Navy escorted Kuwaiti tankers, and in April 1988 it destroyed Iranian oil platforms and warships. On 3 July 1988 the USS Vincennes shot down Iran Air Flight 655, killing all 290 people on board; the US said the crew mistook it for a warplane.

The end: On 18 July 1988 Iran accepted UN Security Council Resolution 598, and a ceasefire took effect on 20 August 1988. Khomeini compared the decision to drinking poison. Estimates of the dead range from several hundred thousand to about a million.

The legacy: Iran fought largely alone under an arms embargo, while Iraq had wide foreign backing. Its leaders drew three lessons: make your own weapons, above all missiles, after the war of the cities; fight enemies far from Iran's borders through allied forces; and rely on the IRGC, which grew up in the war. Many of today's commanders are veterans of it.

items.title: The Revolutionary Guards and the Quds Force
items.sum: The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) was set up in 1979 to protect the revolution and has become Iran's most powerful institution, with its own ground, naval and missile forces, a militia and a large business empire. Its Quds Force runs Iran's operations and allies abroad.
items.detail:
Origins: Khomeini founded the Guards by decree on 5 May 1979 as a force loyal to the revolution, alongside the Shah's former army. They answer to the Supreme Leader, not the president.

Structure: The IRGC has ground, naval and aerospace forces, the last of which controls most of Iran's missiles and drones, plus the Basij militia and the Quds Force. Estimates of its strength range from about 125,000 to 190,000. Its navy patrols the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz with fast attack boats.

The economy: Through its engineering arm Khatam al-Anbiya and linked firms and foundations, the IRGC holds large stakes in oil and gas, construction, ports, telecoms and trade, and profits from moving goods around sanctions. Former commanders hold many senior political posts.

Quds Force: The external branch trains, arms and funds allied groups abroad. Qasem Soleimani led it from about 1998, built Iran's network in Iraq, Syria, Lebanon and Yemen, and directed Iran's role in Syria's civil war and the fight against ISIS in Iraq. A US strike killed him in Baghdad on 3 January 2020, and his deputy Esmail Qaani succeeded him.

Leaders: Hossein Salami, commander from 2019, was killed by Israel on 13 June 2025. His successor Mohammad Pakpour was killed on 28 February 2026. On 1 March 2026 Ahmad Vahidi, a former Quds Force chief and defence and interior minister, was named commander. Argentina accuses Vahidi of a role in the 1994 AMIA bombing in Buenos Aires, which he denies.

Terror listings: The US listed the IRGC as a Foreign Terrorist Organization in April 2019, and Canada listed it in June 2024; several other states have followed.

items.title: The axis of resistance
items.sum: Iran built a network of allied armed groups across the region, which it calls the axis of resistance: Hezbollah in Lebanon, the Houthis in Yemen, militias in Iraq and Palestinian groups in Gaza. Assad's Syria was the land link that held it together until his fall in December 2024.
items.detail:
Hezbollah: Founded in Lebanon in 1982 with the help of IRGC officers after Israel's invasion, it became Iran's strongest ally, with a large arsenal of rockets and missiles. Israel killed its leader Hassan Nasrallah on 27 September 2024, and Naim Qassem succeeded him. Hezbollah opened fire on Israel again on 2 March 2026.

The Houthis: The Ansar Allah movement from northern Yemen took the capital Sanaa in September 2014, and a Saudi-led coalition intervened in March 2015. Iran supplied missile and drone technology. From November 2023 the Houthis attacked shipping in the Red Sea and fired missiles and drones at Israel.

Iraqi militias: Groups such as Kata'ib Hezbollah and Asa'ib Ahl al-Haq were built with Quds Force help. Many joined the state-funded Popular Mobilisation Forces, formed in 2014 to fight ISIS. They have repeatedly attacked US forces in Iraq and Syria.

Palestinian groups: Iran has given money, weapons and training to Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad in Gaza.

Syria: Iran and Hezbollah helped keep Bashar al-Assad in power through the civil war that began in 2011, and Syria was the land route for Iranian arms to Lebanon. On 8 December 2024 rebels led by Hayat Tahrir al-Sham took Damascus and Assad fled to Moscow, cutting that route.

How it works: The Quds Force supplies weapons, money, training and advisers, while each group keeps its own leaders and local aims. This lets Iran put pressure on its enemies from a distance while denying direct responsibility.

items.title: The nuclear programme
items.sum: Iran says its nuclear programme is peaceful, but it enriched uranium to 60%, close to weapons grade, and the UN nuclear watchdog could not confirm it had no military aims. After Israeli and US strikes in 2025 and 2026 most of its enrichment plants are badly damaged, and inspectors have not checked its stockpile since June 2025.
items.detail:
The sites: Natanz is the main enrichment plant, with underground halls. Fordow is a smaller enrichment plant built inside a mountain near Qom. Isfahan holds uranium conversion plants and tunnels used for storage. Arak is a heavy-water reactor that could have made plutonium; its core was removed under the 2015 deal. Bushehr is a Russian-built power reactor, on the grid since 2011.

The reveal: The programme began under the Shah. In August 2002 an exiled opposition group revealed secret sites at Natanz and Arak, and in September 2009 the US, Britain and France exposed Fordow. In 2015 the IAEA concluded that Iran had run a coordinated weapons-related effort until 2003. In 2018 Israel's Mossad took Iran's nuclear archive from a Tehran warehouse.

Enrichment: Power reactors use uranium enriched to 3–5%; weapons use about 90%. The 2015 deal (JCPOA) capped Iran at 3.67% and 300 kg. After the US left the deal, Iran broke the limits from 2019, reached 20% in January 2021 and 60% in April 2021. By June 2025 the IAEA counted about 440.9 kg of 60% uranium, enough for about ten weapons if enriched further.

Breakout: Breakout time is how long it would take to make enough weapons-grade uranium for one bomb. The JCPOA aimed for at least a year; by 2025 US officials put it at one to two weeks. Building a working warhead would take longer.

The IAEA: Iran joined the Non-Proliferation Treaty in 1970. It stopped extra inspections in 2021 and cut cooperation after the June 2025 strikes. On 12 June 2025 the IAEA board found Iran in breach of its obligations, and in September 2026 it referred Iran to the UN Security Council.

Now: Israel and the US struck Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan in June 2025, and the US hit Natanz again on 21 March 2026. In March 2026 the IAEA estimated that just over 200 kg of 60% uranium remained in tunnels at Isfahan, with more at Natanz, but it has not been able to check. On 23 October 2026 IAEA chief Rafael Grossi called for inspectors to return.

items.title: Missiles and drones
items.sum: Iran has the largest and most varied missile force in the Middle East, built mostly at home after the war with Iraq, and it mass-produces cheap attack drones such as the Shahed. It supplies weapons and know-how to its allies, and drones to Russia.
items.detail:
The arsenal: Before the 2025 and 2026 wars, US commanders put Iran's ballistic missiles at more than 3,000. Most belong to the IRGC Aerospace Force, and many are kept in underground bases that Iran calls missile cities.

Ranges: Short-range Fateh-family missiles reach about 300–700 km. Missiles that can reach Israel include the liquid-fuelled Shahab-3, Ghadr and Emad, with ranges of about 1,600–2,000 km, and the solid-fuel Sejjil and Kheibar Shekan. Iran says it limits its range to 2,000 km. It also has cruise and anti-ship missiles and a space launch programme.

Drones: The Shahed-136 is a cheap one-way attack drone with a range of well over 1,000 km, built to be launched in swarms. Larger drones such as the Mohajer-6 and Shahed-129 carry bombs and cameras.

Russia: Since September 2022 Russia has used Shahed drones, which it calls Geran-2, against Ukraine, and it later built them itself at Alabuga in Tatarstan. In September 2024 the US said Iran had sent Fath-360 short-range missiles to Russia; Iran denied it.

The axis: Iran has sent missiles, drones, parts and know-how to Hezbollah, the Houthis, Iraqi militias and Hamas, often for local assembly.

In use: Iran fired more than 300 drones and missiles at Israel in April 2024, more than 180 ballistic missiles in October 2024, and hundreds more in the June 2025 war and since February 2026. Most were intercepted by Israeli, US and allied defences, but some got through.

items.title: The shadow war with Israel
items.sum: For more than a decade before the Gaza war, Israel and Iran fought a covert war: cyberattacks on nuclear plants, killings of scientists, sabotage, attacks on ships and Israeli strikes on Iranian forces in Syria. Israel rarely confirmed its role.
items.detail:
Stuxnet: A computer worm discovered in 2010 damaged about 1,000 centrifuges at Natanz in 2009–2010. It is widely reported to have been built by the US and Israel; neither has confirmed it.

Scientists: Four Iranian nuclear scientists were killed in Tehran between January 2010 and January 2012, several by bombs that motorcyclists stuck to their cars. On 27 November 2020 Mohsen Fakhrizadeh, the senior figure in Iran's past weapons work, was shot dead on a road near Tehran. Iran blamed Israel, which did not comment.

The archive: In January 2018 Mossad agents removed Iran's nuclear archive from a Tehran warehouse. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu revealed the haul on 30 April 2018. Explosions damaged the centrifuge assembly building at Natanz in July 2020 and cut its power in April 2021.

Ships: From 2019 tankers carrying Iranian oil to Syria were hit by mines, and Israeli-linked ships were attacked in turn. At the end of July 2021 a drone struck the Israeli-managed tanker Mercer Street off Oman, killing a British and a Romanian crew member; the US, Britain and Israel blamed Iran, which denied it.

Cyber: In May 2020 a cyberattack disrupted Iran's Shahid Rajaee port, weeks after a reported Iranian attempt to hack Israeli water systems. In October 2021 a cyberattack shut down fuel stations across Iran; a group called Predatory Sparrow claimed this and later attacks.

Syria: From 2017 Israel struck hundreds of Iranian and Hezbollah targets in Syria to stop Iran from entrenching there and moving arms. In February 2018 an Iranian drone flew into Israel from Syria and was shot down.

items.title: Oil, sanctions and the Strait of Hormuz
items.sum: Oil is Iran's main export, and US sanctions since 2018 have pushed most of it to China, sold at a discount through a shadow fleet. Sanctions, war and mismanagement have sent the rial crashing and inflation soaring. The Strait of Hormuz, on Iran's southern coast, carried about a fifth of the world's oil before the war.
items.detail:
Reserves: Iran holds some of the world's largest oil and gas reserves, and shares the giant South Pars gas field with Qatar. Kharg Island handles most of its crude exports.

Sanctions: After sanctions relief in 2016, exports topped 2 million barrels a day. They fell to a few hundred thousand after US sanctions returned in 2018–2019. UN sanctions returned in September 2025.

China and the shadow fleet: In 2025 Chinese refiners bought about 1.38 million barrels a day of Iranian oil, over 80% of its exports, by Kpler's count, mostly small independent refineries known as teapots. The oil moves on ageing tankers that switch off their trackers and transfer cargo at sea, and it is often relabelled as coming from other countries. The US has sanctioned hundreds of these ships.

The rial: A dollar cost 70 rials in 1979 and about 135,000 on the open market in 2018. By late September 2026 it cost about 2.5–2.7 million. Inflation ran around 40% in 2025 and above 80% in 2026. In October 2025 parliament approved removing four zeros from the currency.

Hormuz: The strait links the Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and is about 33 km wide at its narrowest. In 2024 about 20 million barrels of oil a day passed through it, about a fifth of world consumption, plus about a fifth of world LNG trade, mostly from Qatar.

Why it matters: Only Saudi Arabia and the UAE have pipelines that bypass the strait, with about 2.6 million barrels a day of spare capacity. Iran lines its coast and islands, including Abu Musa and the Tunbs, which the UAE claims, with missiles, mines and IRGC fast boats. Since March 2026 traffic has been disrupted by Iranian attacks and a US blockade.

items.title: Protests and the opposition
items.sum: Iran has seen waves of mass protest, each put down by force: the Green Movement of 2009, unrest over prices in 2017–2019, the Woman, Life, Freedom uprising of 2022 and the protests of 2025–2026. The opposition is split between monarchists, the MEK and Kurdish and Baluch armed groups.
items.detail:
2009: Millions protested after Mahmoud Ahmadinejad was declared the winner of the 12 June 2009 election over Mir Hossein Mousavi. The Green Movement was crushed within months, and Mousavi and Mehdi Karroubi have been under house arrest since 2011.

2017–2019: Protests over prices and corruption spread to dozens of towns from December 2017. In November 2019 a sudden fuel price rise set off nationwide unrest; the internet was cut, Amnesty International confirmed at least 304 deaths and Reuters reported about 1,500.

2022: Mahsa (Jina) Amini, a 22-year-old Kurdish woman, died on 16 September 2022 after her arrest by the morality police over her headscarf. Protests led by women and students spread nationwide under the slogan Woman, Life, Freedom. Rights groups counted more than 500 killed, and several protesters were executed.

2025–2026: Protests that began in December 2025 as the rial collapsed were crushed in January 2026; the rights group HRANA counted at least 6,126 dead.

Monarchists and the MEK: Reza Pahlavi, the last Shah's son, lives in the US and calls for a secular, democratic transition. The MEK (People's Mojahedin), a leftist Islamist group that fought the Islamic Republic and sided with Iraq in the 1980s, is led by Maryam Rajavi and based in Albania. Thousands of its members and other prisoners were executed in 1988.

Ethnic groups: Kurdish parties such as the KDPI, Komala and PJAK keep bases in Iraqi Kurdistan, which Iran has struck with missiles and drones. In Sistan and Baluchestan the Sunni militant group Jaish al-Adl attacks security forces. On 30 September 2022 security forces killed dozens of protesters in Zahedan.
